short: How many vehicles pass a point on a road on an average day, counting both directions.
long: AADT is the standard way traffic engineers describe how busy a road is. States count traffic with sensors for a few days or continuously, then adjust for season and day of week to estimate a typical day across the whole year. A city street might carry a few thousand vehicles a day; a downtown interstate can carry over 150,000.

short: The job a road does in the network, from long-distance travel (Interstates) down to reaching your front door (local roads).
long: Planners sort every public road by function. Interstates and other freeways move lots of traffic over long distances with no driveways or stoplights. Arterials carry traffic between and through communities. Collectors gather trips from neighborhoods and feed them to arterials. Local roads give access to homes and businesses. The class affects funding and design standards, and it's why two roads with similar traffic can be built very differently.

short: Which kind of route sign the road carries, such as Interstate, U.S. highway, state highway or county road.
long: Route signing is the shield you see on the road. It mostly reflects who numbered the route, not who maintains it or how busy it is. An unsigned road usually has only a street name. Road type and functional class often line up but not always: a busy city arterial can be unsigned, and some state highways are quiet rural roads.

short: Census survey results pooled over five years, so even small places have enough responses to be reliable.
long: The American Community Survey asks a sample of households every year. Combining five years of responses gives estimates for every county and census tract, at the cost of describing a period (for example 2020–2024) rather than a single year. Small areas have fewer responses, so their estimates are less precise; that's what the margin of error shows.

short: How far the true value could reasonably be from the estimate shown.
long: Survey and model-based numbers are estimates. A value of 12% ± 3% means the true value is likely between 9% and 15%. For Census ACS data the range covers 90% confidence; for CDC PLACES it is a 95% interval. When two places' ranges overlap a lot, the difference between them may not be real.

short: A rate recalculated as if every place had the same age mix, so places with many older or younger residents can be compared fairly.
long: Many health conditions are more common at older ages. Without adjustment, a county full of retirees would look less healthy simply because of its age profile. Age adjustment weights each place's rates to a standard U.S. population, which isolates differences that aren't just about age.

short: A value predicted from survey data and local characteristics rather than counted directly in that place.
long: CDC's PLACES project has health survey responses for states, not for every county. It uses a statistical model that combines those responses with each county's demographics (such as age, race and poverty) to estimate local rates. The estimates are useful for comparison, but they partly reflect the model's inputs, which is why Odd Pairings won't pair them with those inputs.

short: The average of 30 years of weather, here 1991–2020, describing what's typical for a place.
long: A single year's weather is noisy. Climate normals average three decades so they describe the expected climate rather than any one year. They are updated every ten years.

short: A measure of how much heating or cooling a place needs: each day adds how many degrees its average temperature sits below (heating) or above (cooling) 65°F.
long: A day averaging 50°F adds 15 heating degree days; a day averaging 80°F adds 15 cooling degree days. Summed over a year, they track energy demand for heating and air conditioning far better than average temperature does, which is why utilities and building engineers use them.

short: Inspectors rate a bridge's deck, superstructure and substructure from 0 to 9. A bridge is "poor" if its lowest rating is 4 or less.
long: "Poor" does not mean unsafe; unsafe bridges are closed. It means significant deterioration that needs major repair or replacement soon. The map shows the share of bridge deck area (the bridge's surface) in poor condition, the measure the federal government uses, so a big bridge counts more than a small culvert.

short: The total miles driven by all vehicles on an area's roads in a day.
long: VMT multiplies each road's traffic by its length. A county with an interstate running through it can have high VMT even if few people live there, because most of the driving is by people passing through. Dividing by residents makes counties comparable but exaggerates that through-traffic effect.

short: A count scaled to the population, so places of different sizes can be compared.
long: Ten traffic deaths in a county of 10,000 people is a much higher rate than ten in a county of a million. Dividing by population and multiplying by 100,000 puts them on the same footing. In very small counties a single event moves the rate a lot, so treat extreme values there with care.

term: States, counties, tracts, block groups and blocks
short: The nested areas the Census Bureau reports data for. Tracts are neighborhoods of roughly 4,000 people; block groups and blocks are smaller still.
long: Every state is divided into counties (or equivalents), and every county into census tracts. Tracts are drawn to hold about 1,200 to 8,000 people, so they are small in cities and large in rural areas. Each tract splits into a few block groups (usually 600 to 3,000 people), and each block group into blocks, often a single city block. Smaller areas show more detail, but survey estimates for them are less certain (wider margins of error).

short: The number of jobs located in an area, from unemployment-insurance records matched by the Census Bureau.
long: LEHD Origin-Destination Employment Statistics count jobs where they are, not where workers live. They cover most private and public employers but not the self-employed or most federal jobs. Small areas include some statistical noise added to protect confidentiality.

term: How the map colors are grouped
short: Each color holds roughly the same number of places, so the map shows how places rank against each other.
long: Most maps here split places into equal-sized groups (quantiles), from lightest (lowest) to darkest (highest). That makes patterns easy to see, but the value ranges of the groups can be uneven, so always check the legend. Traffic volume uses fixed, conventional ranges instead.

term: Climate and Economic Justice Screening Tool (CEJST)
short: A federal map (2022–2025) that flagged census tracts as "disadvantaged" when they were low income and overburdened in at least one of eight areas.
long: CEJST was built to steer the Justice40 initiative, which aimed 40% of the benefits of certain federal climate and infrastructure programs to disadvantaged communities. A tract qualified if it was at or above a burden threshold in any of eight categories (climate change, energy, health, housing, legacy pollution, transportation, water and wastewater, workforce development) and met the matching low-income threshold, or if it was mostly within tribal lands. The tool and data were removed from federal websites in 2025; this copy comes from the Public Environmental Data Partners mirror of the final 2.0 release.

short: CEJST and USDA's Food Access Research Atlas use the 2010 tract boundaries, which differ in places from the 2020 tracts used by most other layers here.
long: Census tracts are redrawn every ten years. CEJST 2.0 and the 2019 Food Access Research Atlas were built on 2010 tracts, so their tract shapes are drawn as published rather than matched to 2020 tracts. County and state roll-ups use the 2010 county codes, which still match today's counties everywhere except Connecticut (which switched to planning regions in 2022) and a few renamed or split areas.

short: USDA's name for census tracts where incomes are low and many people live far from a supermarket.
long: USDA counts people living more than 1 mile from the nearest supermarket, supercenter or large grocery store in urban tracts, or more than 10 miles in rural ones. A tract is low access when at least 500 people, or a third of residents, live that far, and low income when its poverty rate is 20% or more or its family incomes are well below the area's. Tracts that are both are often called food deserts. Distance isn't everything: a car, transit and prices matter too. The 2019 edition uses 2019 store lists and 2010 Census residents.

short: Agreements that let local police or sheriffs carry out some federal immigration enforcement duties, under ICE supervision.
long: Section 287(g) of the Immigration and Nationality Act lets ICE deputize state and local officers. In the Jail Enforcement model, jail staff check the immigration status of people already booked. In the Task Force model, officers can question and arrest people during regular policing. The Warrant Service Officer model lets jail staff serve ICE administrative warrants. A county with several agreements usually has several agencies (sheriff, city police) signed up. Counts here are agreements, not arrests.

short: The Census asks two separate questions: whether someone is Hispanic or Latino, and their race. People answer for themselves.
long: Because Hispanic origin is asked separately, a Hispanic person can be of any race. These maps count everyone once: Hispanic or Latino residents of any race, then non-Hispanic residents by race ("alone" means one race reported). Those shares add up to 100% for each place. Starting with 2020 data, the Census Bureau codes written-in answers more completely, so more people are counted as two or more races; compare earlier periods with care.

short: The middle value: half of the people, homes or households are above it and half are below.
long: A median isn't pulled up by a few very large values the way an average is, which is why the Census uses it for age, income, home values and rent. A place's median can't be added or averaged with its neighbors' to get a regional median; the county and state values here are computed from the full data, not from their tracts.

short: Dollar amounts are restated in 2024 dollars, so earlier periods can be compared without inflation getting in the way.
long: The Census Bureau reports each 5-year period in its own last year's dollars. When you step back to earlier periods on the map, those values are converted to 2024 dollars with the Consumer Price Index (CPI-U), so a change you see reflects a real change in buying power rather than rising prices.

short: A score for income inequality from 0 (every household earns the same) to 1 (one household has all the income).
long: The Gini index summarizes how far a place's household incomes are from being equal. Most U.S. counties fall between about 0.35 and 0.55. A higher value means a wider gap between high- and low-income households; it says nothing about whether a place is rich or poor overall, so read it next to median income.

short: The labor force is everyone working or actively looking for work. The unemployment rate is the share of them without a job.
long: Retirees, students and others not looking for work are outside the labor force, so they don't count as unemployed. That's why a place can have low unemployment and also few people working. These survey figures are averaged over five years, so they won't match the monthly rates in the news from the Bureau of Labor Statistics.

short: A renter household is "burdened" when rent and utilities take 30% or more of its income.
long: The 30% line is the long-standing federal benchmark for housing affordability (HUD). Households spending more than half their income are considered severely burdened. Households with no income or no cash rent are left out because the share can't be computed.

short: A household where nobody 14 or older speaks only English or speaks it "very well."
long: The Census Bureau uses this to find households that may need help in other languages, for example with public notices, voting materials or emergency alerts. It is about the household as a whole: one fluent teenager or adult is enough for the household not to count. The Census Bureau regrouped this table in 2016, so this map starts with 2015–2019.

short: A count of every person and home, not a survey sample, so there's no margin of error.
long: The decennial Census counts every resident and housing unit as of April 1, 2020. Its redistricting file (P.L. 94-171) is published down to census blocks, often a single city block. To protect privacy, the Census Bureau adds statistical noise to small-area counts (differential privacy), so a single block's numbers can be off by a few people; block groups and larger areas are reliable.

short: The share of a household's income that goes to home energy bills: electricity, gas and heating fuels.
long: A household earning $40,000 that spends $2,400 a year on home energy has a 6% burden; 6% or more is commonly called high, and 10% or more severe. These figures are modelled, not actual bills: the Department of Energy fits incomes and energy costs from the 2018–2022 American Community Survey to each tract's homes and heating fuels, then scales bills to what local utilities reported selling. An area's value is its average yearly bill divided by its average household income. Gasoline for cars isn't included.

short: The yearly income line the federal government uses to define poverty, set by household size: $27,750 for a family of four in 2022.
long: Many aid programs use multiples of it: "200% of poverty" means twice the line, about $55,500 for a family of four in 2022, and is a common cut-off for energy bill help and weatherization. The line is the same across the lower 48 states (higher in Alaska and Hawaii), so it doesn't adjust for local costs: a household just under it in an expensive city is often worse off than one in a cheaper rural area.

short: The President's finding that a disaster is too big for a state or tribe to handle alone, which opens up federal aid.
long: A governor or tribal leader asks, FEMA reviews the damage, and the President decides. The declaration lists the counties that qualify for aid to rebuild public facilities, help households and reduce future risk. Smaller emergency declarations (often before a hurricane lands) and fire management declarations are separate and aren't counted here. More declarations can mean more damage, but also a state that asks more often or costs that clear federal thresholds more easily, so it isn't a direct measure of losses.

short: FEMA's nationwide model of how much 18 natural hazards are expected to cost each county and census tract, and how well people there could cope.
long: The National Risk Index combines decades of hazard records (floods, wildfires, hurricanes, tornadoes, heat waves, earthquakes and more) with what is in harm's way (buildings, people and crops) to estimate average yearly losses, then adjusts for social vulnerability and community resilience to give an overall risk score. It's a model built for national comparisons and planning, not a record of what happened or a substitute for a local risk assessment. Version 1.20 (December 2025) isn't comparable with version 1.19.

short: The average yearly cost of a hazard over the long run: a bad year costs far more and most years far less.
long: FEMA multiplies how often a hazard strikes, what's exposed to it and how much of that is typically lost, adding up damage to buildings and crops plus deaths and injuries. Deaths and injuries are turned into dollars using the federal value of a statistical life (about $13.7 million per death in this version), so in places with few buildings, or for hazards like heat that mostly harm people, they can make up most of the total. Mapwich divides FEMA's figure by the number of residents so large and small places can be compared.

short: A 0–100 national rank: a county scoring 90 has higher risk than 90% of counties. It ranks places; it doesn't measure risk in absolute terms.
long: FEMA's risk score starts from expected annual loss, raises it where social vulnerability is high and lowers it where community resilience is high, then ranks every county (and separately every tract) against the rest of the country. Because it's a rank, a small change in one place can move others, and a new version can move scores even where the hazards didn't change.

short: How much harder a disaster would hit people here because of things like low income, disability, crowding, no car or no health insurance.
long: In version 1.20 of FEMA's National Risk Index, social vulnerability comes from the Census Bureau's Community Resilience Estimates, which count residents facing several of about ten risk factors (low income, living alone or with a single caregiver, crowded housing, limited English, no full-time worker, disability, no health insurance, age 65 or older, no vehicle, no broadband). Earlier versions used CDC's Social Vulnerability Index instead. The score is a 0–100 national rank; higher means more vulnerable.

short: How well a community is equipped to prepare for, absorb and recover from disasters. Higher is better.
long: FEMA's National Risk Index takes community resilience from the University of South Carolina's Baseline Resilience Indicators for Communities (BRIC), which combines measures of social, economic, housing and infrastructure, institutional, community and environmental capacity. It's a 0–100 national rank among counties; FEMA gives every census tract its county's score, so Mapwich shows it for counties only.

short: CDC's ranking of every county and census tract by how hard a disaster or disease outbreak would hit the people who live there.
long: It combines 16 census measures in four themes: socioeconomic status; household characteristics (age, disability, single parents, limited English); racial and ethnic minority status; and housing type and transportation. The overall score ranks places on all 16 together, so it isn't an average of the four theme ranks. Emergency planners use it to decide where help is needed first. It describes residents, not the hazards they face. Where CDC has no value (its code -999, mostly tracts with no residents), the map shows no data.

short: Where a place falls among all others, from 0 to 100: the 75th percentile means higher than 75% of places.
long: A percentile rank only says how places compare, not how much of something there is. CDC ranks every county against all U.S. counties, and every tract against all U.S. tracts, not just those in the same state, so a tract can be low for its state and still rank high nationally, or the other way round. Because it's a rank, a place can move when others change even if it didn't.

short: The number EPA uses to judge whether a county's air meets the federal standard: a three-year average at the county's worst monitor.
long: Air pollution swings from day to day and year to year, so EPA smooths it. For fine particles (PM2.5) the design value is the yearly average concentration, averaged over three years. For ozone it is the fourth-highest daily peak (8-hour average) each year, averaged over three years. A county's value comes from its single highest valid monitor, so it describes the worst-measured spot, not the average resident's exposure. Counties with no valid monitor have no value, which does not mean the air is clean. Days EPA excludes as exceptional events, such as wildfire smoke, are left out.

short: The federal legal limit for an air pollutant. Design values above it mean the county does not meet the standard.
long: Under the Clean Air Act, EPA sets a limit for each common pollutant. The annual fine-particle (PM2.5) standard is 9.0 micrograms per cubic meter, tightened from 12.0 in 2024. The 8-hour ozone standard is 0.070 parts per million. A county whose design value is above the limit is violating the standard, which can lead to a formal "nonattainment" designation and cleanup requirements. The tables are informational and are not themselves a regulatory determination.
